title: Is More Information Better? The Effects of Report Cards on Health Care Providers
research_question: How does the public disclosure of provider-level patient health outcomes for cardiac surgery affect the matching of patients to providers, the quantity and incidence of intensive cardiac procedures, health care expenditures, and patient health outcomes? In particular, do such disclosures improve or harm patient and social welfare, and do effects differ between healthier and sicker patients?
data_description: The study uses two main data sources covering 1987-1994. The first is comprehensive longitudinal Medicare claims data on essentially all elderly (65+) beneficiaries admitted with a new primary diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) or for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, yielding roughly 1.77 million AMI patient-year observations and about 968,000 CABG patient-year observations. Patient-level variables include demographics (age, gender, race, rural residency), prior-year inpatient hospital expenditures and days (illness severity proxies), receipt of CABG, angioplasty (PTCA), and catheterization within 1 day, 30 days, and 1 year of admission, total hospital expenditures in the year after admission, readmissions with AMI or heart failure, and one-year mortality. The second source is the American Hospital Association annual survey, providing hospital size, ownership, teaching status, and rural location for nonfederal general medical/surgical hospitals.
institutional_context: The setting is the introduction of mandatory, publicly released hospital- and surgeon-specific report cards on risk-adjusted CABG surgery mortality in two U.S. states. New York's Department of Health began releasing hospital-specific raw and risk-adjusted CABG mortality in December 1990, adding surgeon-specific mortality in 1992. Pennsylvania's Health Care Cost Containment Council began publishing hospital- and surgeon-specific risk-adjusted CABG mortality in November 1992. These programs were considerably more clinically detailed than discharge-abstract-based reporting systems used by HCFA (nationally since 1986) and by states such as California and Wisconsin. Because CABG is largely elective, providers can potentially respond to public outcome rankings by selecting healthier patients, while risk adjustment cannot fully capture unobserved severity. The institutional question is whether such mandated public disclosure improved provider quality and patient sorting or instead induced selection that harmed sicker patients.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: EVENT STUDY — treatment = providers with report cards, control = providers without report cards; shock/instrument/cutoff = introduction of report cards

key_variables.treatment: introduction of report cards for healthcare providers
key_variables.outcome: provider performance metrics and patient health outcomes
key_variables.time_period: several years before and after report card introduction

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The introduction of report cards had negative welfare effects overall: providers engaged in cream-skimming (avoiding severely ill patients) and the sickest patients experienced worse outcomes. While some process-of-care measures improved, the net effect on patient welfare was harmful, particularly for high-risk patients.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Significant increase in adverse selection; mortality for high-risk CABG patients increased after report card introduction
key_robustness: alternative specifications of the time window
